lead: A cooling tower is an evaporative cooler for water. Hot water falls through packing while air rises or crosses. A small fraction of the water evaporates and carries latent heat away, so the rest leaves colder. For large heat loads this is cheaper than a closed heat exchanger. Power stations, refineries, petrochemical plants and big air-conditioning systems use cooling towers to reuse cooling water. The design is set by enthalpy, not by a plain temperature difference: the wet-bulb temperature fixes the lowest water temperature, and the Merkel integral converts the required cooling into fill volume.
prereq: You need 7.3 for wet-bulb temperature and 7.4 for the air-water enthalpy balance; the mass transfer coefficient topic supplies the coefficients behind Ka.

sections.h3: What a cooling tower does and how it is built

blocks.text: A cooling tower rejects heat from circulating water to air. Hot water is sprayed over a fill. Air passes through the fill. A small part of the water evaporates, and the latent heat leaves with the vapour. The remaining water becomes colder. This is not a closed heat exchanger; the cooling comes from evaporation.

items: Natural-draught atmospheric towers rely on wind and a chimney effect. Natural-draught hyperbolic towers use a tall concrete shell to create draught; large power stations use them.

Mechanical-draught towers use fans: forced-draught towers blow air in at the bottom, induced-draught towers pull it out at the top. Induced draught is more common, because the warm, humid exhaust leaves fast and is not drawn back into the inlet.
Counter-flow towers have water falling down and air rising up. Cross-flow towers have water falling down and air moving horizontally.

Construction: fill or packing gives thin films and large contact area; nozzles distribute hot water; drift eliminators catch droplets; louvers guide air; the fan moves air; the cold water basin collects cooled water.

blocks.text: Range is hot-water temperature minus cold-water temperature. Approach is cold-water temperature minus entering-air wet-bulb temperature. For 40 °C hot, 30 °C cold and 24 °C wet bulb, range is 10 K and approach is 6 K. The wet bulb is the lower limit because evaporation cannot cool water below it. A smaller approach needs a larger fill. Dry-bulb temperature alone does not set the size.

sections.h3: Enthalpy driving force and the Merkel equation

blocks.text: At any level, water loses heat L cp dT and air gains enthalpy G dh. For constant L/G, air enthalpy changes linearly with water temperature: h = h1 + (L cp/G)(T − Tc). The local driving force is h* − h. Here h* is the saturation enthalpy of air at the water temperature. h is the bulk air enthalpy at that level.

blocks.where: L is water mass flow in kg/s; c<sub>p</sub> is water specific heat, about 4.187 kJ/(kg K); dT is a small water temperature change in K; G is dry-air mass flow in kg/s; dh is the small air enthalpy change in kJ/kg dry air.

blocks.text: KaV/L = c<sub>p</sub> ∫ dT/(h* − h) from Tc to Th
blocks.where: KaV/L is the tower characteristic, dimensionless; c<sub>p</sub> is water specific heat, 4.187 kJ/(kg K) when h is in kJ/kg dry air and T is in K, and this factor is what makes KaV/L dimensionless; K is the mass transfer coefficient, a is interfacial area per unit volume, V is fill volume in m³, L is water flow in kg/s; Tc and Th are cold and hot water temperatures; h* is saturation enthalpy at the water temperature and h is bulk air enthalpy, both in kJ/kg dry air.

blocks.text: KaV/L is the number of transfer units, NTU. With fill height Z, Z = HTU × NTU and HTU = L/(Ka A), where A is the tower cross-sectional area in m²; then HTU is in metres and Z comes out in metres. The tower characteristic depends on L/G: more air per kg water lowers h at the same water temperature, raises h* − h, and lowers KaV/L, but fan power rises. Manufacturers give KaV/L against L/G for each fill.

A four-point Chebyshev estimate uses four fixed nodes: evaluate 1/(h* − h) at T = Tc + 0.1R, Tc + 0.4R, Tc + 0.6R and Tc + 0.9R, where R = Th − Tc, and take KaV/L ≈ c<sub>p</sub> R/4 times the sum. For three equally spaced points, Simpson's rule is KaV/L ≈ c<sub>p</sub> (Th − Tc)/6 [f<sub>bottom</sub> + 4 f<sub>mid</sub> + f<sub>top</sub>], where f = 1/(h* − h).

sections.h3: Water losses, blowdown and fan power

blocks.text: Evaporation loss is E = G(Y2 − Y1), where Y1 and Y2 are inlet and outlet air humidity in kg water/kg dry air. Pure water leaves and salts stay, so dissolved solids concentrate. Blowdown B is deliberate drain. With cycles of concentration N and negligible drift, B ≈ E/(N − 1). More cycles save water but raise scaling risk.

Fan power is P ≈ Q<sub>air</sub> Δp/η, where Q<sub>air</sub> is air volume flow in m³/s, Δp is fan pressure rise in Pa, and η is fan efficiency. Higher air flow lowers L/G, which lowers the tower characteristic and so can reduce fill size, but fan power rises.

figure.caption: The worked example on an enthalpy–temperature plot. The curve is h*, the enthalpy of air saturated at the water temperature; the straight line is the air, rising from 72.2 to 118.7 kJ/kg dry air with slope L c<sub>p</sub>/G = 4.65. The vertical gaps h* − h at 30, 35 and 40 °C, 27.5, 33.6 and 47.4 kJ/kg, are the Merkel driving forces; Simpson's rule on their inverses gives KaV/L = 1.23.

spec.aria: Plot of enthalpy against water temperature from 28 to 42 degrees. A rising curve for saturated air lies above a straight air operating line. Vertical bars at 30, 35 and 40 degrees mark driving forces of 27.5, 33.6 and 47.4. A side panel lists the tower data and the result 1.23.

examples.question: A tower cools 1.0 kg/s of water from 40 °C to 30 °C. Air enters at a wet bulb of 24 °C and leaves at about 38 °C; dry-air flow is 0.9 kg/s. Saturation enthalpies h* at 30, 35 and 40 °C are 99.7, 129.0 and 166.9 kJ/kg dry air. Inlet air has h1 = 72.2 kJ/kg and Y1 = 0.0189 kg/kg dry air; outlet air has Y2 = 0.031 kg/kg dry air. Find the heat load, the tower characteristic and the evaporation loss.
steps: Air enthalpy rise: dh = Q/G = 41.87/0.9 = 46.52 kJ/kg dry air. Outlet enthalpy h2 = 72.2 + 46.52 = 118.7 kJ/kg dry air.
Bottom driving force: h* at 30 °C is 99.7; h1 is 72.2; h* − h = 99.7 − 72.2 = 27.5 kJ/kg.
Middle: water at 35 °C, h* = 129.0; air enthalpy h = 72.2 + 46.52/2 = 95.5; driving force = 129.0 − 95.5 = 33.6 kJ/kg.
Top: h* at 40 °C is 166.9; h2 is 118.7; driving force = 166.9 − 118.7 = 48.2 kJ/kg.
Evaporation: E = G(Y2 − Y1) = 0.9 × (0.031 − 0.0189) = 0.0109 kg/s ≈ 40 kg/h. This is 0.0109/1.0 × 100 = 1.1 % of circulation.
examples.answer: The heat load is 41.9 kW, the tower characteristic is about 1.2 (dimensionless), and evaporation is about 0.011 kg/s (roughly 40 kg/h, 1.1 % of circulation).

traps: Using dry-bulb temperature in the approach. Approach uses the entering-air wet-bulb temperature.
Using a water-air temperature difference as the Merkel driving force. The driving force is h* − h, an enthalpy difference in kJ/kg dry air.
Mixing range and approach: range = hot water − cold water; approach = cold water − wet bulb.
Evaluating h* at the air temperature instead of at the water temperature at that level.
Using wet-air flow instead of dry-air flow G in the air enthalpy and evaporation balances.

quiz.q: Define range and approach for a cooling tower.
quiz.a: Range = hot-water temperature − cold-water temperature. Approach = cold-water temperature − entering-air wet-bulb temperature.

quiz.q: Why does the wet-bulb temperature, not the dry-bulb temperature, set the lowest water temperature?
quiz.a: Evaporative cooling stops when air is saturated at the wet-bulb temperature; below that no evaporation driving force remains. Dry bulb alone does not give the lower limit.

quiz.q: A tower cools water from 38 °C to 29 °C; wet bulb is 23 °C. Find range and approach.
In the Merkel integral, why is h* taken at the water temperature?
quiz.a: The water surface is effectively saturated at the water temperature, so h* is the saturation enthalpy of air in equilibrium with that water. The difference h* − h drives heat and mass transfer.

quiz.q: What happens to tower characteristic KaV/L when L/G increases at fixed water temperatures?
quiz.a: When L/G increases there is less air per kg of water, so the air enthalpy h is higher at the same water temperature, h* − h is smaller, the integral is larger and KaV/L increases (a taller or larger fill is needed). Fan power falls, since less air is moved.

quiz.q: State the job of the fill and the drift eliminator.
quiz.a: Fill creates thin water films and large contact area. Drift eliminator catches water droplets so they are not carried out with air.

quiz.q: Two towers have the same range but approaches 2 K and 8 K. Which needs more fill?
quiz.a: The 2 K approach tower needs more fill. Its cold water is closer to the wet bulb, so h* − h is smaller and the integral, hence KaV/L, is larger.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern towers use film fills, low-noise fans, variable-speed drives and plume-abatement coils. Hybrid towers switch between dry and wet operation when water is scarce. Cooling-water treatment controls scale, corrosion and Legionella risk. Search 'Merkel number cooling tower', 'cooling tower blowdown cycles' and 'cooling tower acceptance test' for practice.
